## Factual research brief — `javax.net.ssl.SSLContext` / `SSLContextSpec`

### 1. What `SSLContext` governs, and what this finding refers to

`javax.net.ssl.SSLContext` is a JSSE engine class representing a secure-socket-protocol implementation. An instance is a factory for `SSLSocketFactory`, `SSLServerSocketFactory`, and `SSLEngine`, and it holds shared state such as session state for objects created from it. It is initialized with key managers, trust managers, and a secure-random source. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

The message **“the observed call sequence is not one SSLContextSpec accepts”** refers to the static-analysis rule’s accepted event trace and its declared predicates—not to a documented Java runtime exception, a TLS handshake result, an enabled-protocol list, or a negotiated TLS version. The supplied CrySL source permits the order `Get, Init, Engine?`, declares `getDefault()` forbidden, constrains the `getInstance` protocol value, and requires three analysis predicates for the `init` arguments. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

Accordingly, based on the rule source, a finding can result from any of the following rule-level conditions:

- the trace does not match **Get → Init → optional Engine**;
- `getDefault()` is observed;
- the value associated with `protocol` is not proven to be exactly `"TLSv1.2"` or `"TLSv1.3"`;
- the `init` arguments do not satisfy `generatedKeyManagers[km]`, `generatedTrustManagers[tm]`, or `randomized[random]`.

The raw rule does **not** contain the detector presentation text “InvalidSequenceOfMethodCalls,” nor does it identify which particular condition produced a particular diagnostic. Without the detector’s raw diagnostic, version, and compiled-rule artifact, the precise failed condition is unresolved.

A requested `SSLContext` algorithm name must also not be confused with the protocol ultimately enabled or negotiated. Oracle documents that an `SSLContext` returned for a requested protocol can implement other protocols as well; the protocols actually enabled are controlled on the created socket or engine, including via `setEnabledProtocols` or `SSLParameters.setProtocols`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html)) Therefore, the CrySL literal constraint on `getInstance(...)` is not a runtime finding that TLS 1.2 or TLS 1.3 was—or was not—enabled or negotiated.

### 2. Officially documented API usage and remediation guidance

Oracle’s API documentation describes the following usage semantics:

- Obtain a new context through one of the `SSLContext.getInstance(...)` overloads, with a standard protocol name and, optionally, a provider. With no provider specified, the registered provider list is searched; with a provider specified, the requested provider supplies the implementation. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))
- A newly obtained context is initialized with `init(KeyManager[] km, TrustManager[] tm, SecureRandom random)`. The API explicitly permits either manager array to be `null`; installed providers are then used to locate the relevant implementation. It also permits a `null` `SecureRandom`, in which case a default implementation is used. The API does **not** require non-null custom manager arrays or a caller-created random source. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))
- A context that requires initialization can reject socket-factory or `SSLEngine` creation before `init()` with `IllegalStateException`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))
- `SSLContext.getDefault()` is documented as returning an immediately usable default context that does not require initialization. This is API-valid behavior, notwithstanding the CrySL rule’s separate prohibition of `getDefault()`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))
- For an `SSLEngine`, Oracle recommends explicitly selecting client or server mode with `setUseClientMode(...)` before other engine operations because the default is provider-specific. Connection-specific configuration should be completed before the handshake begins. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))
- `SSLParameters` represent allowed connection protocols, cipher suites, endpoint identification, SNI, client authentication, and related connection properties, and may be applied to an `SSLEngine` or socket. Oracle states that a non-empty endpoint-identification algorithm requires endpoint identification/verification during the handshake and identifies that as protection against man-in-the-middle attacks. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLParameters.html))

**Documented remediation when used otherwise:** The official `SSLContext` API documentation does not prescribe a CrySL-specific correction, does not say to replace `"TLS"` with a version literal, does not say to avoid `getDefault()`, and does not say that `init(null, null, null)` is invalid. Its direct operational guidance is that a newly created context should be initialized before operations that require an initialized context, and that an appropriate provider-supported protocol name must be supplied to `getInstance(...)`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

In particular, the official sources do not justify weakening trust management, certificate validation, or endpoint identification to satisfy a static predicate. The CrySL predicates are provenance requirements in the rule; they are not Java API requirements or a runtime proof of certificate or hostname-validation behavior.

### 3. Compatibility, formats, version support, and migration

**Persisted formats.** The reviewed official `SSLContext` API and JSSE guide describe in-memory context and session state, including cached sessions shared by objects created under the same context. They do not document an `SSLContext` persistence, serialization, or on-disk format, nor a persisted-format migration path for changing the `getInstance(...)` algorithm string or initialization style. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html))

**Wire behavior.** The protocol name supplied to `SSLContext.getInstance(...)` requests an implementation; it does not alone state the complete set of wire versions that will be enabled or the version that will be negotiated. The standard-name specification says that `"TLS"` supports some TLS version and *may* support other SSL/TLS versions; similarly, version-specific names such as `"TLSv1.2"` and `"TLSv1.3"` may support other SSL/TLS versions. Oracle further documents that enabled protocols are controlled on the resulting `SSLSocket`, `SSLServerSocket`, or `SSLEngine`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html))

Changing protocol configuration can therefore affect peer interoperability at handshake time. Oracle’s JSSE guide identifies incompatible peer protocol support as a possible handshake issue and lists `SSLContext.getInstance`, `SSLEngine.setEnabledProtocols`, `SSLSocket.setEnabledProtocols`, and `SSLParameters.setProtocols` among the configuration points. Its legacy fallback discussion warns that fallback to earlier versions normally reduces security strength and is not suggested unless truly necessary and understood. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html))

**Platform-version support.** In the Java SE 25 API documentation, every Java-platform implementation is required to support `TLSv1.2` and `TLSv1.3`; additional protocol support is implementation- and release-dependent. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html)) The Java SE 11 `SSLContext` documentation lists `TLSv1`, `TLSv1.1`, and `TLSv1.2` as platform-required protocols and advises consulting release documentation for others. That historical documentation difference shows why compatibility must be checked against the actual Java runtime and provider, rather than inferred only from source-level API use. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

**Documented migration path.** No formal API migration path is documented for changing a generic `"TLS"` context request, a default context, or null `init` arguments into the particular literal/provenance requirements imposed by this CrySL rule. The official sources distinguish context creation from connection-level enabled-protocol configuration; they do not prescribe a blanket conversion to a version-pinned context. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html))

### 4. Exact matching rule in `SSLContext.crysl`

The governed type is stated at the top of the supplied rule:

> `SPEC javax.net.ssl.SSLContext`

The rule’s matching and condition clauses, quoted verbatim, are:

```text
FORBIDDEN
    getDefault() => Get;

EVENTS
    g1: getInstance(protocol);
    g2: getInstance(protocol, _);
    Get := g1 | g2;

    i1: init(km, tm, random);
    Init := i1;

    se1: eng = createSSLEngine();
    se2: eng = createSSLEngine(_,_);
    Engine := se1 | se2;

ORDER
    Get, Init, Engine?
CONSTRAINTS
    protocol in {"TLSv1.2", "TLSv1.3"};

REQUIRES
    generatedKeyManagers[km];
    generatedTrustManagers[tm];
    randomized[random];
```

([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

The same source declares these object types:

```text
java.lang.String protocol;
javax.net.ssl.KeyManager[] km;
javax.net.ssl.TrustManager[] tm;
javax.net.ssl.SSLEngine eng;
java.security.SecureRandom random;
```

([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

From that source:

| Rule event | Matched method form | Parameter constraint stated by the rule |
|---|---|---|
| `Get` | `getInstance(protocol)` or `getInstance(protocol, _)` | First argument is the declared `java.lang.String protocol`; second argument in the two-argument form is unconstrained (`_`). The subsequent constraint requires `protocol in {"TLSv1.2", "TLSv1.3"}`. |
| `Init` | `init(km, tm, random)` | Three arguments correspond to declared `KeyManager[]`, `TrustManager[]`, and `SecureRandom` objects. The rule requires the three named predicates. |
| `Engine` | `eng = createSSLEngine()` or `eng = createSSLEngine(_, _)` | Zero arguments, or two unconstrained arguments. Return is associated with declared `javax.net.ssl.SSLEngine eng`. |
| forbidden event | `getDefault()` | No arguments; explicitly forbidden and mapped syntactically to `Get` with `=> Get`. |

The rule then ensures `generatedSSLContext[this] after Init` and `generatedSSLEngine[eng] after Engine`. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

**Receiver type / same-name question:** No—the source does not describe a name-only rule that applies merely because some unrelated method is named `getInstance`, `init`, `createSSLEngine`, or `getDefault`. It declares one governed specification type, `javax.net.ssl.SSLContext`, and its event method names are declared within that specification. The raw rule contains no clause extending matching to arbitrary receiver types with methods of the same names. The source alone does not further specify CrySL dispatch, inheritance, aliasing, or analysis-engine matching semantics beyond that type declaration.

### Source URLs

- Oracle Java SE 25 `SSLContext` API:  
  `https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html`
- Oracle Java SE 25 `SSLParameters` API:  
  `https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLParameters.html`
- Oracle Java SE 25 JSSE Reference Guide:  
  `https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html`
- Oracle Java SE 25 Standard Algorithm Names — `SSLContext` algorithms:  
  `https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html#sslcontext-algorithms`
- Oracle Java SE 11 `SSLContext` API:  
  `https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html`
- CrySL rule source reviewed:  
  `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl`

**Source limitations:** The CrySL URL uses the mutable `master` branch and the supplied SHA-256 was not independently verified against a downloaded artifact here. The source also does not define the detector UI label, identify the precise failed predicate for this report, or document the detector’s treatment of values that cannot be statically resolved.
